standard.title: Civic and global participation
standard.description: how and why individuals and groups, including community, religious and cultural groups, participate in and contribute to civic life in Australia and to global citizenship
standard.prior_knowledge: Students know how culture and religion influence individuals' and groups' perceptions and expressions of citizenship (AC9HC8K05), and have examined debates about national identity and citizenship (AC9HC8K06). They understand that citizenship is expressed through identity and culture but have not yet examined formal and informal mechanisms of civic participation at community, national and global levels.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain how and why individuals and groups participate in civic life in Australia and as global citizens, including the contribution of community, religious and cultural organisations.

nodes.label: Forms and motivations of civic participation
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify different forms of civic participation and explain the motivations that lead individuals and groups to participate.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least two different forms of civic participation (e.g. voting, volunteering, activism, charitable work) and explain why individuals or groups participate.
nodes.typical_width: Describe formal and informal forms of civic participation; explain motivations for participation including community responsibility, religious obligation, cultural identity, and personal commitment; distinguish between local, national and global levels of civic engagement.
wider: Investigate historical examples of civic movements in Australia (e.g. the 1967 referendum campaign, women's suffrage) and compare their methods and motivations with contemporary civic participation
Compare the civic participation frameworks in Australia with another democracy and assess how institutional structures shape participation
Examine barriers to civic participation for marginalised groups and evaluate strategies that have increased inclusion

response_modes.reason: Students tend to think of civic participation as voting or protesting. Building a broader repertoire of participation forms — including volunteering, faith-based service, online advocacy, community organising — provides the range needed for Node 2's case analysis.

success_criteria: Names at least two different forms of civic participation at different levels (local, national, or global)
Explains at least one motivation that leads an individual or group to participate civically

nodes.label: Community, religious and cultural groups in civic life
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can research and explain the contribution of specific non-government organisations, community or religious groups to Australian civic life.
nodes.minimum_width: Research one specific Australian NGO, community group or religious organisation and explain its contribution to civic life.
nodes.typical_width: Research the work of Australian NGOs, philanthropists, community groups and religious groups; explain the extent to which they contribute to the Australian community; include examples from different types of organisations (faith-based, secular, community-led); consider how different groups respond to different community needs.
wider: Compare the civic contributions of a faith-based organisation (e.g. Salvation Army, Sikh Volunteers Australia) with a secular NGO (e.g. Red Cross, Oxfam) and evaluate how their motivations and methods differ
Investigate an organisation that specifically supports First Nations Australian communities and assess how it complements or fills gaps in government services
Examine how the SES or another emergency volunteer organisation contributes to civic resilience and evaluate what makes its model effective

response_modes.reason: Students who research only one type of organisation tend to generalise its model to all civic participation. Examining two or three contrasting organisations (e.g. one faith-based, one secular, one focused on First Nations communities) develops more nuanced understanding of the diversity of civic contribution.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The range of Australian civic organisations is rich — from major national NGOs to grassroots community groups to diaspora organisations — and offers advancing students multiple contexts for evaluating what makes civic contribution effective and sustainable.
success_criteria: Describes the work of at least one specific Australian NGO, community or religious group
Explains the extent of its contribution to civic life with reference to a specific activity or outcome

nodes.label: Global citizenship
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain what global citizenship means and provide examples of individuals or groups acting as global citizens.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain what it means to be a global citizen and identify one example of a person or group acting as a global citizen.
nodes.typical_width: Research examples of young people acting as global citizens (e.g. Malala Yousafzai, Greta Thunberg, Amelia Telford, Bassam Maaliki); explain what distinguishes global citizenship from national civic participation; discuss how global citizenship connects to issues such as sustainability, climate change, and human rights.
wider: Investigate the work of UNICEF Youth Ambassadors or equivalent programs and evaluate how they build global citizenship capacity in young people
Examine a global citizenship campaign on a sustainability or climate issue and assess what made it effective or ineffective at driving change
Compare the concept of global citizenship across different cultural frameworks and evaluate whether it is a universal or Western-centric concept

response_modes.reason: Global citizenship risks being abstract without concrete examples. Using examples of young Australians alongside international figures makes the concept accessible and avoids the misconception that global citizenship requires celebrity status.

success_criteria: Explains what global citizenship means in their own words
Identifies at least one example of an individual or group acting as a global citizen and explains what makes their actions an expression of global citizenship
